article_title: Are Two Algebra Classes Better Than One? The Effects of Double-Dose Instruction in Chicago
citation: Claire Durwood, Emily Krone, and Christopher Mazzeo. (2010). Are Two Algebra Classes Better Than One? The Effects of Double-Dose Instruction in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research, University of Chicago. http://ccsr.uchicago.edu/content/page.php?cat=3&content_id=34
title: Ability grouping can be effective when accompanied by deep supports for teachers
description: The brief argues that tracking, widely condemned for creating weak instructional environments, can benefit students when regrouping is paired with substantial instructional supports. In Chicago, "lower-skilled students benefited from more instructional time and better resources provided for their teachers," while higher-skilled students gained from more homogeneous classes. The general lesson offered is that "curriculum reforms like double-dose are more likely to succeed when they include the kinds of deep supports for teaching provided in this instance."
requirements: Extended instructional time, curricular resources, and professional development on instructional practice must accompany the regrouping
constraints: Students with the weakest skills, especially those in special education, were least well served and need differentiated support
target_learners: Ninth-grade students with below-median entering math skills
Higher-skill ninth-grade students
target_learning_goals: Algebra skills and course performance in high school mathematics
examples: Chicago schools divided freshmen by eighth-grade test scores into single-period and double-period algebra, with district professional development workshops three times a year and new curricular materials for double-dose teachers
key_sources: Claire Durwood, Emily Krone, and Christopher Mazzeo. (2010). Are Two Algebra Classes Better Than One? The Effects of Double-Dose Instruction in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research, University of Chicago. http://ccsr.uchicago.edu/content/page.php?cat=3&content_id=34

article_title: Ready to Succeed in the Classroom: Findings from Teacher Discussion Groups on Their Experiences and Aspirations Teaching Students in the Foster Care System
citation: The Center for the Future of Teaching and Learning. (2010). Ready to Succeed in the Classroom: Findings from Teacher Discussion Groups on their Experiences and Aspirations Teaching Students in the Foster Care System. Prepared for the Stuart Foundation. https://www.cftl.org
title: California Assembly Bill 490 (2004): education rights and district responsibilities for students in foster care
description: AB490 (Steinberg), Chapter 862, became law in January 2004 and establishes specific education rights for children and youth in foster care in California and responsibilities for school personnel, judges, attorneys, social workers, probation officers, and caregivers. Its provisions are designed to give these students access to the same educational opportunities and resources as other students. Provisions include the ability to finish the school year in the school of origin, immediate enrollment even without records, school records transferred within 2 days, and full or partial credits for previous coursework accepted by schools.
requirements: Every school district must appoint an Educational Liaison to ensure that students in the foster care system have access to these services
constraints: Some teachers in the discussion groups were not aware of the education-specific rights AB490 provides
target_learners: Children and youth in the California foster care system
target_learning_goals: Continuous enrollment and credit accumulation across placement changes
Access to the same educational opportunities as other students
examples: The National Center for Youth Law's website offers AB490-specific resources, including roles and responsibilities for specific audiences and an implementation guide for schools
key_sources: The Center for the Future of Teaching and Learning. (2010). Ready to Succeed in the Classroom: Findings from Teacher Discussion Groups on their Experiences and Aspirations Teaching Students in the Foster Care System. Prepared for the Stuart Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED511840

article_title: Modeling AI Overreliance as a Complex Adaptive System
citation: Ahana Biswas. (2026). Modeling AI Overreliance as a Complex Adaptive System. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19616
title: AI reliance as a complex adaptive system: a micro-founded agent-based model of population-level reliance dynamics
description: The article models AI reliance as a population process rather than a one-shot individual judgment. Agents repeatedly choose among solving alone, accepting AI output unverified, or verifying, updating Dirichlet beliefs about AI quality and, when networked, learning from peers through experience-based or opinion-dynamics channels. As the authors put it, "individual learning rules, peer observation, and feedback exposure jointly determine whether a population remains calibrated or enters a self-reinforcing state of unverified reliance." The model is used as a theoretical tool for isolating mechanisms and deriving qualitative comparative statics, not as a point forecast.
requirements: A population of heterogeneous agents facing repeated tasks with the core learning loop, in which "belief→action→outcome→updated belief" drives choice; the cascade results additionally require a networked peer channel and a social-proof feedback term entering the unverified-use utility.
constraints: "AI quality is exogenous and stationary, the network fixed, and verification stylized."
The model is a theoretical tool for isolating mechanisms rather than a point forecast; its implications are qualitative and conditional, doubling as testable hypotheses.
target_learners: professionals repeatedly using AI assistants for information-seeking and decision tasks
target_learning_goals: calibrated reliance on AI assistance — trusting it when right and checking it when wrong
examples: The model's components are mapped to a running example of a professional using an AI assistant who may answer alone, accept the AI's answer, or check it, and who sees colleagues increasingly accept AI answers unchecked.
key_sources: Ahana Biswas. (2026). Modeling AI Overreliance as a Complex Adaptive System. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19616

article_title: Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem
citation: Jaidka K and Cai M. (2026). Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem. Front. Psychol. 17:1935527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935527
title: Two-dimensional user typology: ability to verify and motivation to verify yield four profiles with distinct calibration risks
description: The article collapses Hoff and Bashir's three layers of trust in automation into two functional dimensions: "The ability to verify rests on domain expertise and AI literacy," while motivation draws on need for cognition and epistemological beliefs. Crossing the dimensions yields four profiles: high-both users near calibrated trust, high-ability/low-motivation users at risk of complacent overtrust, low-ability/high-motivation users whose checks misfire, and low-both users most exposed to overtrust. Profiles are positions, not identities, and shift across tasks.
requirements: Design interventions must be matched to profiles, since the question is not simply whether an intervention works but for whom
constraints: The typology is deliberately simple and the boundaries between profiles are soft
target_learners: Chatbot users varying in domain expertise, AI literacy, and motivation
target_learning_goals: Matching trust-calibration interventions to user profiles
examples: Figure 1 maps each calibration risk to the intervention families most likely to address it
key_sources: Jaidka K and Cai M. (2026). Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem. Front. Psychol. 17:1935527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935527

article_title: Nonverbal Reasoning as a Contributor to Sentence Recognition Outcomes in Adults With Cochlear Implants
citation: Mattingly Jameson K MD, Castellanos Irina PhD, Moberly Aaron C MD. (2018). Nonverbal Reasoning as a Contributor to Sentence Recognition Outcomes in Adults with Cochlear Implants. Otology & Neurotology. https://doi.org/10.1097/MAO.0000000000001998
title: Abbreviated 12-item Raven's Progressive Matrices assessment for clinical prediction of sentence recognition
description: A shortened computerized version of the Raven's Progressive Matrices consisting of the 12 test items that significantly differentiated low- versus high-performing CI users on PRESTO sentence recognition. The article states this "abridged version of the RPM, consisting of only twelve test items instead of the standard 48 items, should be able to be completed in only three to four minutes and may have clinical utility in predicting post-operative performance." It was validated by correlations with sentence recognition in both CI users and normal-hearing controls listening to noise-vocoded speech.
requirements: Administered visually on a touch screen monitor with 3×3 matrices of geometric designs and eight response boxes; requires near vision better than 20/40
constraints: The article states additional studies are needed to determine the test's prognostic utility in CI users, and that correlations are moderate rather than deterministic
target_learners: Post-lingually deafened adults considering or using cochlear implants
target_learning_goals: Predicting degraded speech recognition outcomes from nonverbal reasoning to guide counseling and rehabilitation planning
examples: CI users were categorized as low vs. high performers via a median split on PRESTO whole sentences (cut point 21.67%), and Fisher's Exact Tests on individual RPM items identified the 12-item subset
key_sources: Mattingly Jameson K MD, Castellanos Irina PhD, Moberly Aaron C MD. (2018). Nonverbal Reasoning as a Contributor to Sentence Recognition Outcomes in Adults with Cochlear Implants. Otology & Neurotology. https://doi.org/10.1097/MAO.0000000000001998

article_title: CSCL in Asia
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2011). CSCL in Asia. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 6:1–7. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9112-1
title: Abduction and collaborative hypertext as support for multi-faceted classroom inquiry
description: Glassman and Kang present the logic of inquiry — sometimes called abduction in contrast to deduction and induction — as discussed by Dewey and Peirce. Rather than arguing from initial facts to a single conclusion, "abduction involves exploring multiple possibilities suggested by an observation." They propose that computer-supported collaboration media like wikis and blogs could support such multi-faceted inquiry, with collaborative hypertext providing an alternative to traditional linear deductive thinking and supporting complex networks of knowledge exploration, hearkening back to hypertext notions of Engelbart and Nelson.
requirements: Computer-supported collaboration media such as wikis and blogs further developed to support multi-faceted inquiry
constraints: The editorial questions why blogs and wikis should be singled out rather than extensions of discussion forums like Knowledge Forum or WebGuide
target_learners: School students in student-centered inquiry classrooms
target_learning_goals: Innovative thinking and exploration of multiple possibilities from observations
examples: The authors review student experiences in the Philippines, Japan, Taiwan, and Korea taking first steps in Dewey-style student-centered inquiry
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2011). CSCL in Asia. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 6:1–7. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9112-1

article_title: Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning
citation: Lucas Paulsen, Jacob Davidsen. (2025). Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09446-7
title: ABC-VR: a conceptual framework for collaborative 360VR learning grounded in activity theory
description: ABC-VR is a conceptual framework for designing and researching IVR-mediated collaborative learning, grounded in activity theory and practice theory. It builds on "a dual sense of activity" — the original activity recorded with 360-degree cameras and the collaborative learning activity learners produce in an ABC-VR session. It shifts attention from individual concepts like immersion and presence to group-level meaning-making, where learners "question each other and imagine future actions" and figuratively reason with participants in the original activity.
requirements: Relies on software allowing shared playback of 360-degree video in HMDs, such as CAVA360VR, with tools for pausing, scrubbing and annotating
constraints: Knowledge produced in 360VR remains 'on-action' (Schön, 1983) because recorded activities cannot be manipulated owing to reduced interactivity of 360VR
target_learners: higher education students
professional learners such as teachers and medical students
target_learning_goals: collaborative analysis and reflection on recorded real-world practices
examples: Illustrated via medical knee examination training, mentoring of newly qualified teachers, and a speculative psychiatric multidisciplinary meeting case
key_sources: Lucas Paulsen, Jacob Davidsen. (2025). Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09446-7

article_title: Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning
citation: Lucas Paulsen, Jacob Davidsen. (2025). Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09446-7
title: Three collaboration modes for ABC-VR: within-VR, outside VR, and across realities
description: ABC-VR does not limit collaboration to one mode. Within IVR, learners are jointly immersed and can pause, annotate and discuss the recording; outside VR, IVR serves as an individual or shared interactional resource, with learners taking off headsets in a co-located space; across realities, one learner is immersed while others follow on a screen, allowing non-immersed learners to guide the immersed learner in real time. A screen mediates across realities, making the immersed learner's interaction visible to others.
requirements: Software supporting shared playback, pausing, scrubbing and annotation for within-VR mode; a screen-based mediator across realities for the third mode
constraints: Across-realities collaboration limits the immersed learner's access to the bodily conduct of non-immersed learners, risking fractured ecologies
target_learners: immersed learners and their non-immersed peers or mentors
examples: Silseth et al. (2024) used individual 360VR experiences as interactional resources for collaboration outside IVR; Paulsen et al. (2022) and Steier (2020) explored across-realities collaboration
key_sources: Lucas Paulsen, Jacob Davidsen. (2025). Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09446-7

article_title: Enhancing learning of nanoscale phenomena: the role of agent-based models and embodied reasoning
citation: Polly K. Lai. (2026). Enhancing learning of nanoscale phenomena: the role of agent-based models and embodied reasoning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09776-x
title: Use manipulable agent-based models rather than passive visualization videos when the learning goal is explanatory and transferable understanding of invisible, emergent phenomena
description: The article recommends instructional designs that leverage embodied processes for complex scientific phenomena. Because ABMs let students "manipulate individual agents and observe system-level outcomes" while engaging perspective taking, causal inference, and motor-supported thinking, they are better suited than pre-structured videos when the goal is mechanistic explanation and transfer; videos remain adequate for declarative facts. The principle rests on the study's finding that both formats supported declarative knowledge but only ABMs fostered significant explanatory gains and transfer.
requirements: ABM environments must allow parameter manipulation and observation of emergent agent interactions
Time-on-task and informational content should be equated across formats, as the study did
constraints: Evidence comes from a single 27-participant study in nanoscience with undergraduates; declarative knowledge showed no advantage for ABMs
target_learners: undergraduate STEM students learning abstract, invisible phenomena
examples: Students worked with two NetLogo ABMs (Nano Gold, Nano Magnetics) covering the same concepts and duration as comparison videos, then completed identical pre/post-tests and think-aloud tasks
key_sources: Polly K. Lai. (2026). Enhancing learning of nanoscale phenomena: the role of agent-based models and embodied reasoning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09776-x

article_title: Researchers under the spell of the arts: Two decades of using arts-based methods in community-based inquiry with vulnerable populations
citation: Sara Coemans, Karin Hannes. (2017). Researchers Under the Spell of the Arts: Two Decades of Using Arts-Based Methods in Community-Based Inquiry with Vulnerable Populations. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.08.003
title: Definition and classification framework for arts-based methods in community-based inquiry
description: The review proposes a shared definition to address the "confusing plethora of terms" in the field: "The use of artistically inspired methods by researchers and participants in a collaborative research environment where members of the community are actively involved either in creating art in the search for meaning or in providing a critical, situated response to artistically inspired formats of research dissemination from others." It also distinguishes research about art, art as research, and art in research, including only the latter in the review. ABR methods operate as data collection techniques, where art forms are data in their own right, or as dissemination vehicles replacing traditional textual reports.
requirements: Researchers or participants actively create art or respond critically to artistic dissemination within a collaborative community research environment
constraints: The review's definition covers art in research projects only, excluding art therapy and medically inspired projects
target_learners: community members and vulnerable populations participating in community-based inquiry
target_learning_goals: expressing experiences that are difficult to verbalize
examples: The review included only studies meeting its art in research definition, where art is used in one or more phases of a research process with active researcher involvement
key_sources: Sara Coemans, Karin Hannes. (2017). Researchers Under the Spell of the Arts: Two Decades of Using Arts-Based Methods in Community-Based Inquiry with Vulnerable Populations. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.08.003

article_title: Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods
citation: Jason C. Chow · Ruben G. Martinez. (2026). Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10152-5
title: AI synthesis tools such as Abstrackr for machine-assisted evidence synthesis
description: The article notes that "Artificial intelligence (AI) methods for evidence synthesis are on the rise" and cites Abstrackr (Wallace et al., 2012) as synthesis software that has "leveraged natural language" processing for synthesis tasks. It appears in a section on leveraging AI within CAPERS, positioning AI tools as complements to community-integrated synthesis processes. The supplied text is truncated mid-description of this section.
requirements: AI tools support but do not replace the participatory integration decisions CAPERS specifies
constraints: The article's discussion of AI is introductory; the supplied text truncates before full treatment
target_learners: Synthesis teams in educational psychology
target_learning_goals: Increase efficiency of screening and synthesis workflows
examples: Abstrackr cited as an example of synthesis software using natural language methods
key_sources: Jason C. Chow · Ruben G. Martinez. (2026). Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10152-5

article_title: How Learners’ Visuospatial Ability and Different Ways of Changing the Perspective Influence Learning About Movements in Desktop and Immersive Virtual Reality Environments
citation: Birgit Brucker, Georg Pardi, Fabienne Uehlin, Laura Moosmann, Martin Lachmair, Marc Halfmann, Peter Gerjets. (2024). How Learners' Visuospatial Ability and Different Ways of Changing the Perspective Influence Learning About Movements in Desktop and Immersive Virtual Reality Environments. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09895-w
title: Ability-as-enhancer versus ability-as-compensator assumptions for visuospatial ability as an instructional moderator
description: The article presents two alternative assumptions about how learners' visuospatial ability moderates the effectiveness of instructional formats. Under the ability-as-compensator assumption, well-designed formats such as dynamic visualizations act as compensatory tools enabling lower-visuospatial-ability learners to reach similar outcomes to higher-ability learners. In contrast, "the ability-as-enhancer assumption suggests that learners with higher visuospatial ability might even be able to utilize specific instructional formats, even if these formats are less optimally designed", for example by more accurately imagining how to rotate a model to an optimal viewing position. The study's research question R1 asks which assumption fits the observed moderation.
requirements: Both assumptions presuppose that visuospatial ability is measured as a continuous learner factor (here via the paper folding test)
constraints: The article treats these as alternative assumptions to be explored, not as settled findings
target_learners: learners varying in visuospatial ability
target_learning_goals: learning about movements with dynamic visualizations and 3D-models
examples: Study 1 explored whether visuospatial ability acts as compensator or enhancer by testing interaction format × visuospatial ability interactions on learning outcomes
key_sources: Birgit Brucker, Georg Pardi, Fabienne Uehlin, Laura Moosmann, Martin Lachmair, Marc Halfmann, Peter Gerjets. (2024). How Learners' Visuospatial Ability and Different Ways of Changing the Perspective Influence Learning About Movements in Desktop and Immersive Virtual Reality Environments. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09895-w

article_title: The Reliability, But Not the Cronbach’s Alpha, of Knowledge Tests Matters: Response to Zitzmann and Orona (2025)
citation: Peter A. Edelsbrunner, Bianca A. Simonsmeier, Michael Schneider. (2025). The Reliability, But Not the Cronbach's Alpha, of Knowledge Tests Matters: Response to Zitzmann and Orona (2025). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10023-5
title: Abandon fixed alpha cutoff values for knowledge tests; report alpha and its confidence interval for studying item interrelatedness instead
description: The article recommends that fixed cutoff values for knowledge tests' alphas be abandoned because they do not ensure reliability and instead increase publication bias. Researchers should still report alpha and its confidence interval, but as indices of item interrelatedness rather than reliability. As the authors conclude: "Fixed cutoff values for the alphas of knowledge tests must be abandoned because they do not ensure reliability but instead increase publication bias." Methodological rigor instead requires flexible, theory-guided application of methods.
requirements: Researchers should still report alpha and its confidence interval for knowledge tests to derive and study item interrelatedness
constraints: The recommendation applies to heterogeneous constructs like knowledge; alpha remains appropriate as a reliability index for homogeneous constructs
target_learners: Educational researchers
Test developers
examples: The authors contrast the homogeneous Satisfaction with Life Scale, where alpha is meaningful, with the heterogeneous bMCU mechanics knowledge test, where it is not
key_sources: Peter A. Edelsbrunner, Bianca A. Simonsmeier, Michael Schneider. (2025). The Reliability, But Not the Cronbach's Alpha, of Knowledge Tests Matters: Response to Zitzmann and Orona (2025). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10023-5

article_title: An absolute point scale for the group measurements of intelligence. Part I.
citation: Otis, A. S. (1918). An absolute point scale for the group measurements of intelligence. Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 9(5), 239-261. https://books.google.com/books/about/the_journal_of_educational_psychology.html
title: The Absolute Point Scale framework and the Coefficient of Brightness: ability units defined so equal point increments equal ability increments and zero points mean absence of ability
description: The framework holds that scores from different tests can be averaged fairly only after transmutation into common absolute units, or points, such that equal increments of ability receive equal increments of points. Otis defines the Coefficient of Brightness as "the quotient that would be obtained by dividing the measure of the absolute amount of mental ability of any individual by the measure of the absolute amount of mental ability which was normal for the age of that individual." The scale's zero is set so that zero points represent "just absence of ability," and the framework was applied in this study by dividing each pupil's total point score by the age norm taken from the curve of Fig. 2.
requirements: Measures must be in terms where equal increments of ability are measured by equal increments of the scale and twice as many units represent twice as much ability
Age norms must be available for the pupil's age, taken from the smoothed curve for fractional ages
constraints: Reliable norms were obtained only for ages 10 to 14; the straight line to age zero was an assumed extrapolation, and norms above age 15 are only roughly approximate because older pupils were selected
target_learners: pupils in grades 4 to 8 of the elementary school
target_learning_goals: measuring general mental ability on an absolute scale and comparing individuals to age norms
examples: Each pupil's coefficient of brightness was found by dividing his total point score by the score normal for his age, with norms for fractional ages read from the Fig. 2 curve
key_sources: Otis, A. S. (1918). An absolute point scale for the group measurements of intelligence. Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 9(5), 239-261. https://books.google.com/books/about/the_journal_of_educational_psychology.html

article_title: Debiasing Education Algorithms
citation: Jamiu Adekunle Idowu. (2024). Debiasing Education Algorithms. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00389-4
title: ABROCA: Absolute Between-ROC Area fairness metric
description: ABROCA is a fairness metric proposed by Gardner et al. (2019) and adopted by several reviewed studies. "This metric measures the absolute value of the area between the baseline group ROC curve ROCb and the comparison group(s) ROCc. The lower the ABROCA value, the less unfair the algorithm." Unlike threshold-dependent metrics such as equalized odds, ABROCA evaluates model discrimination across all thresholds and can be computed directly from prediction modeling results with minimal computational requirement.
requirements: Requires ROC curves for a baseline group and comparison group(s) from a prediction modeling task
constraints: The review notes ABROCA might not be as effective in scenarios where specific decision thresholds are crucial
target_learners: student subgroups evaluated by predictive models (e.g., MOOC learners, dropout-prediction students)
target_learning_goals: measuring subgroup discrimination in student dropout, performance, and forum post classification models
examples: S6 (Sha et al., 2021) used ABROCA to assess fairness of students' forum post classification; S2 (Sha et al., 2022) used it for dropout prediction, performance prediction, and forum post classification
key_sources: Jamiu Adekunle Idowu. (2024). Debiasing Education Algorithms. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00389-4

article_title: A meta-analysis of technology-delivered literacy instruction for elementary students
citation: Dahl-Leonard, K., Hall, C., & Peacott, D. (2024). A meta-analysis of technology-delivered literacy instruction for elementary students. Education Tech Research Dev (2024) 72:1507–1538. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10354-0
title: ABRACADABRA web-based literacy program
description: ABRACADABRA (A Balanced Approach for Children Designed to Achieve Best Results for All) is a publicly available, web-based literacy program that was the most frequently evaluated program in this meta-analysis's corpus, used in 12 of the 50 publicly available treatment conditions. The article states it "was developed based on the recommendations of the NRP (2000) report and targets a range of skills, including phonological awareness, phonics, vocabulary, comprehension, fluency" and that its "Activities in ABRACADABRA can be customized to a student's specific abilities and challenges." The article cites a meta-analysis of 17 ABRACADABRA studies estimating a weighted average effect of g = 0.26.
requirements: Delivered on a technological device as technology-delivered instruction; in this corpus it was implemented in school settings on computers/laptops
constraints: The g = 0.26 figure is attributed to Abrami et al. (2020), a separate meta-analysis, not computed in this article
target_learners: Elementary students in Grades K-5
Students with or at risk for reading difficulties
examples: 12 of the 50 publicly available treatment conditions in the corpus used ABRACADABRA, with total instructional hours ranging from 6 to 33 in Table 4
key_sources: Dahl-Leonard, K., Hall, C., & Peacott, D. (2024). A meta-analysis of technology-delivered literacy instruction for elementary students. Education Tech Research Dev (2024) 72:1507–1538. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10354-0

article_title: BE COOL! a digital learning environment to challenge and socially include gifted learners
citation: Tessa H. S. Eysink, Alieke M. van Dijk, Ton de Jong. (2020). BE COOL! a digital learning environment to challenge and socially include gifted learners. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09754-9
title: The ability-adjusted jigsaw method: combining heterogeneous design groups with ability-matched expert groups
description: The ability-adjusted jigsaw method unites learning by design, learning together, and inquiry learning. Children of varying ability levels work in heterogeneous design groups on a complex, open-ended problem; each child is responsible for one topic, with topic assignment depending on ability level. Members split into homogeneous expert groups of similar ability who "are responsible for becoming experts about the same topic" via inquiry assignments matched to their level, then return to share and integrate knowledge in the design group. The method is adapted from the original jigsaw procedure of Aronson et al. (1978) and is intended to serve both cognitive and socio-emotional needs of gifted and non-gifted children.
requirements: A complex, open-ended design problem requiring knowledge of multiple topics
Topic assignment matched to children's ability levels
Homogeneous expert groups with inquiry assignments matched to ability level
constraints: The article notes elementary school children may experience problems with knowledge sharing and integration, which may be amplified when children differ in knowledge level and pace of learning, hence the worksheet support
target_learners: Gifted, average-ability, and low-ability children in grades 4 to 6 of primary education
target_learning_goals: Science inquiry skills (light and heat, oxygen, water, nutrition)
Design and justification of a solution to an authentic problem
Collaborative knowledge sharing across ability levels
examples: A seven-week science lesson series for grades 4–6 in which children design a liveable house on the moon for a family of four
key_sources: Tessa H. S. Eysink, Alieke M. van Dijk, Ton de Jong. (2020). BE COOL! a digital learning environment to challenge and socially include gifted learners. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09754-9

article_title: The Effect of Inquiry-Based Learning Method on Students' Academic Achievement in Science Course
citation: Ali Abdi. (2014). The Effect of Inquiry-based Learning Method on Students’ Academic Achievement in Science Course. Universal Journal of Educational Research 2(1): 37-41. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2014.020104
title: 30-item teacher-made Academic Achievement Test for fifth-grade science
description: The study's outcome instrument was a teacher-made Academic Achievement Test administered as pre-test and post-test to both groups. It "included 30 multiple-choice items", each with one correct answer and three distracters, based on a table of specification organized for three chapters of the sciences education course. Content validity was examined by two science teachers, one researcher and one university professor, and internal consistency was reported.
requirements: Content validity checked by expert panel; based on a table of specification for the taught chapters
constraints: Teacher-made test covering only the three course chapters taught during the eight-week experiment
target_learners: fifth-grade primary school students
examples: Cronbach's alpha of the test was found to be 0.75
key_sources: Ali Abdi. (2014). The Effect of Inquiry-based Learning Method on Students’ Academic Achievement in Science Course. Universal Journal of Educational Research 2(1): 37-41. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2014.020104

article_title: Teaching Probability to Pre-Service Teachers with Argumentation Based Science Learning Approach
citation: Ömer Sinan Can, Tevfik İşleyen. (2016). Teaching Probability to Pre-Service Teachers with Argumentation Based Science Learning Approach. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.33. https://www.iiste.org
title: Argumentation Based Science Learning (ABSL) approach
description: The ABSL approach, originally named the Science Writing Heuristic, is a constructivist-based instructional method in which students determine research questions, design activities, develop claims, support them with evidence, and defend results in small and large group discussions. The article describes it as built on constructivist learning theory and requiring guided inquiry activities, interactive group work, meaning via collective negotiated exchange of ideas and argumentation, and reflective writing. Its argumentation structure follows Toulmin's model, in which data, claims, and warrants are mandatory and backing, rebuttals, and qualifier increase the validity of the argument.
requirements: Guided inquiry activities, interactive group work, negotiated exchange of ideas and argumentation, and reflective writing, per the format the article describes
constraints: The article describes the approach as applied within instructional sequences; its reported use here is limited to teaching probability to pre-service teachers over five weeks
target_learners: pre-service elementary school mathematics teachers
examples: In this study, groups of 4-6 students proposed claims for sample questions, defended them before other groups, and negotiated solutions moderated by researcher questions
key_sources: Ömer Sinan Can, Tevfik İşleyen. (2016). Teaching Probability to Pre-Service Teachers with Argumentation Based Science Learning Approach. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.33. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1122873

article_title: Teaching Probability to Pre-Service Teachers with Argumentation Based Science Learning Approach
citation: Ömer Sinan Can, Tevfik İşleyen. (2016). Teaching Probability to Pre-Service Teachers with Argumentation Based Science Learning Approach. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.33. https://www.iiste.org
title: ABSL lesson pattern of group claim generation, public defence, and cross-group negotiation
description: A recurring lesson-level design in which students first form self-selected groups of 4-6 people, propose their own claims for a sample question on the blackboard, and solve questions by agreeing and discussing within the group. A group spokesman writes the solution on the blackboard while supporting claims with applicable information, and must convince the other groups, who support or invalidate the claim with solid evidence. The researcher fosters negotiation with questions such as "Do you agree with your friend's solution? Why?" and closes each example by summarizing the agreed solution.
requirements: Time allocated per question must account for the length and complexity of the sample question and the group discussions, as the article states
constraints: The article notes ABSL lessons required more lesson time than traditional lessons due to the long duration of debate between groups
target_learners: pre-service elementary school mathematics teachers
target_learning_goals: constructing and defending claims with evidence
examples: The implementation took five weeks, with 20 lessons in the experimental group and 18 in the control group, each averaging 45 minutes

It states "it is important to give place t o the ABSI approach in science education programs." Successful application is conditioned on developing teachers' knowledge and skill in the approach.

constraints: The supporting study found no significant between-group post-test difference, so the achievement benefit is evidenced only as a within-group gain.

target_learning_goals: science conceptual understanding in the unit of reproduction, growth, development in living beings
examples: Over five weeks, two 6th grade classes were taught the unit via argumentation following Ministry of National Education acquisitions while one control class received non-intervened teaching, with lessons tape-recorded and a 20-question achievement test administered as pre- and post-test.

citation: Wehman P, Schall CM, McDonough J, Graham C, Brooke V, Riehle JE, Brooke A, Ham W, Lau S, Allen J, Avellone L. (2017). title: Applied behavior analytic instructional techniques embedded across classroom and internship settings
description: The PS-ASD model increased the structure and intensity of Project SEARCH learning experiences by ensuring the use of applied behavior analytic techniques throughout classroom instruction and internship supports. Techniques include "scored task analyses for teaching multistep tasks, structured repeated trials for discrete tasks, behavioral rehearsal for specific social skills, visual and self-directed prompting procedures for transitioning, self-management procedures for behavioral challenges, and reinforcement for appropriate behavior," with regular data review, functional behavior assessment, and customized employment to match tasks to intern strengths.
requirements: Trained staff: treatment site staff received additional training and coaching in the supports, and instructional and behavioral plans were adjusted based on regular review and analysis of data
constraints: The article states the intervention requires a higher degree of detailing in the manual
target_learners: Transition-aged youth with autism spectrum disorder with significant support needs
examples: Table 1 maps activities such as classroom orientation, internship rotations, and business development to methods including video modeling, functional communication training, scripting, and time delay

article_title: ABRA: Online Reading Support. Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Sandra McNally, Jenifer Ruiz-Valenzuela and Heather Rolfe. (2016). ABRA: Online Reading Support — Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. http://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN18254678
title: ABRA (Abracadabra) web-based balanced literacy programme and its matched non-ICT paper-and-pencil version
description: ABRA is a 20-week online literacy programme of phonic fluency and comprehension activities built around age-appropriate electronic texts, delivered by a teaching assistant to groups of three to five pupils in four 15-minute sessions per week. The report describes it as "a modular 'game'-based balanced literacy intervention that is fixed in content". The non-ICT version matched every ABRA activity with a paper-and-pencil equivalent using the same stories, vocabulary, questions, words and letter sounds, differing only in delivery medium. Average cost per pupil per year over three years was £8.52 (ICT) and £8.49 (non-ICT), frontloaded into the first year.
requirements: Delivery by a trained teaching assistant in small groups of three to five pupils, four 15-minute sessions per week over 20 weeks
Training of TAs (1.5 days plus ongoing support) prior to and during implementation
constraints: Content is fixed; new activities cannot and will not be added
Writing activities exist in ABRA but were not included in the 20-week programme evaluated
target_learners: Year 1 pupils in English primary schools, including disadvantaged pupils
target_learning_goals: Early literacy: phonic fluency, word reading, and reading comprehension
examples: In the trial, 48 schools and 1,884 pupils were included in the final analysis, with pupils randomised to ABRA, the non-ICT intervention, or standard literacy provision

article_title: Promoting Alternative Thinking Strategies (PATHS): Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Alexandra Barlow, Michael Wigelsworth, Ann Lendrum, Kirsty Pert, Craig Joyce, Emma Stephens, Lawrence Wo, Garry Squires, Kevin Woods, Rachel Calam, Mark Harrison, Alex Turner, and Neil Humphrey. (2015). Promoting Alternative Thinking Strategies (PATHS) Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: The Affective-Behavioural-Cognitive-Developmental (ABCD) model underpinning PATHS
description: The ABCD model is the developmental theory on which the PATHS curriculum is based. It "emphasizes the developmental integration of a ffect, emotion language, behaviour and cognitive understanding to promote social and emotional co mpetence". The programme logic model proposes that core components (a taught curriculum, generalisation activities and techniques, and parent materials) decrease risk factors such as impulsive behaviour and increase protective factors, leading to improved emotion knowledge, self-control and social problem-solving, with academic attainment viewed as a by-product of implementation.
requirements: Delivery of the core programme components: a taught curriculum, generalisation activities and techniques, and parent materials
constraints: In this trial the model's distal academic outcome was not realised: PATHS showed no positive impact on attainment
target_learners: Primary school children from Reception to Year 6 in mainstream classes
target_learning_goals: Social and emotional competence, including emotion knowledge, self-control and social problem-solving
examples: PATHS lessons in this trial were delivered twice-weekly in 30-40 minute sessions by class teachers, supplemented by generalisation activities and send-home parent materials

description: The article describes five speaking activities drawn from Holmes (2003) and the British Council's E.T.T.E project: a pair interview ("Getting to Know You Interview"), the command game "Simon Says", a tactile guessing game ("It's in the Bag"), an impromptu one-minute team speaking game, and a lie-detecting question game ("Detective"). Warm-up activities "help the students get to know each other in a comfortable atmosphere" and come in two types: pair interviews with little teacher supervision, and fun games.

A guideline sheet, a bag of about twenty everyday items, or impromptu topics as materials
constraints: Context-appropriate topics were suggested for the Pakistani classroom, such as the electric power shortage crisis

article_title: Implementing Argumentation-Based Science Learning Approach in Social Studies: Academic Achievement and Students' Views
citation: Akbaş, Y.; Şahin, İ. F.; Meral, E. (2019). Implementing Argumentation-Based Science Learning Approach in Social Studies: Academic Achievement and Students' Views. Review of International Geographical Education Online (RIGEO), 9(1), 209-245. https://doi.org/10.33403/rigeo.529139
title: Argumentation-Based Science Learning (ABSL) approach
description: ABSL is a learning approach that aims to cultivate students as individuals with strong social, collaboration and communication skills who "critically evaluate arguments and justifications in discussions". Its structure helps students formulate questions, practice claims and provide evidence, and "create arguments with effective reasoning". The article applies it in seventh-grade social studies, organizing lessons around activities such as concept cartoons, competing theories, predict-observe-explain, and news analysis within 5E model steps.
requirements: Students work through argumentation activities individually and in groups, sharing, defending, and discussing claims with argument components
constraints: The article notes the approach had been mostly used in science education and only limitedly in social studies, and students needed familiarization and experienced initial difficulties
target_learners: seventh-grade middle school students
examples: An 8-week implementation in which groups of five students created individual arguments, defended them with argument components, and group reporters shared arguments in whole-class discussions

article_title: Integrating Argument-Based Science Inquiry with Modal Representations: Impact on Science Achievement, Argumentation, and Writing Skills
citation: Demirbag, M., & Gunel, M. (2014). Integrating Argument-Based Science Inquiry with Modal Representations: Impact on Science Achievement, Argumentation, and Writing Skills. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 14(1), 386-391. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2014.1.1632
title: Argument-Based Science Inquiry (ABSI) classroom pattern
description: ABSI, adopted from the Science Writing Heuristic, is a "language-enriched student-centered learning environment" that "aims to provide a scaffolding structure to promote science literacy." Students generate research questions, design investigations, collect data, generate evidence, form claims, and reflect, then share arguments in small or large group discussions and complete activity reports displaying question, design, claim, evidence, and reflections. Instructors regulate questions within the curriculum, encourage sharing, and create oral and written negotiation environments.
requirements: An instructor and lab assistants to regulate research questions and facilitate negotiation environments
Activity reports after each investigation as written artifacts of the argument structure
constraints: Studied in third-year college science education sections; effects on other populations not established
target_learners: college science education students
examples: In all sections, students ended the implementation with a writing-to-learn activity and a poster communicating their understanding to middle school students.

article_title: Effect of Ability Grouping in Reciprocal Teaching Technique of Collaborative Learning on Individual Achievements and Social Skills
citation: Sumadi, I. N. S. Degeng, Sulthon, & Waras. (2017). Effect of Ability Grouping in Reciprocal Teaching Technique of Collaborative Learning on Individual Achievements and Social Skills. International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education, 6(3), 216-220.
title: Ability-grouping composition as an instructional-design variable in collaborative learning
description: The article frames grouping composition (homogeneous vs. heterogeneous) as a manipulable instructional-design variable within collaborative learning. Homogeneous groups can be "divided into high group of homogeneous, middle group of homogeneous, and the lower group of homogeneous", each with distinct psychological dynamics: low and middle homogeneous groups experience low competition and mental pressure but lack high-ability peers to push them upward, while high-ability groups face high competition. Heterogeneous grouping allows upper-ability members to contribute to lower-ability members but may weigh down the upper group. This framework organizes the study's comparison of four compositions.
requirements: Deliberate identification of learners' ability levels before group assignment, as the article states "The way to do is to set the initial conditions of a group, namely with the process of identification of learners properly"
constraints: The article notes the framework's trade-offs: "upper group weighed down or even interrupted its development by having to help or wait for the progress lower group" in heterogeneous groups, and lack of upward push in low homogeneous groups
target_learners: Primary School Teacher Education Department students (pre-service teachers)
examples: The study operationalized the framework by comparing high, middle, and low homogeneous groups against a heterogeneous group within reciprocal teaching of collaborative learning.
key_sources: Sumadi, I. N. S. Degeng, Sulthon, & Waras. (2017). Effect of Ability Grouping in Reciprocal Teaching Technique of Collaborative Learning on Individual Achievements and Social Skills. International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education, 6(3), 216-220. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1157151

article_title: From image to clinical judgment: a randomized near-peer teaching trial on systematic chest radiograph interpretation.
citation: Yepes-Velasco Andres Felipe, Solano Andres, Hernandez Jorge, Mora-Salamanca Andrés Felipe, Moreno-Araque Jeimy Lorena. (2026). From image to clinical judgment: a randomized near-peer teaching trial on systematic chest radiograph interpretation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08971-9
title: ABCDE systematic CXR interpretation checklist
description: The intervention's core artifact is a systematic assessment tool for chest x-ray interpretation built on the ABCDE mnemonic (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure). The article states it was "developed using the ABCDE mnemonic for systematic CXR interpretation, as previously described in the literature", and the full checklist is provided in Supplementary Material S1. It scaffolds visual search to organize exploration and reduce omissions in novice readers.
requirements: Delivered as a one-hour lecture-only session introducing the checklist; no guided practice or supervised hands-on application was included in either arm
constraints: The checklist was taught by intensive care medicine residents who had completed a one-month radiology rotation during PGY-2, which the authors say is likely important for content accuracy and instructional credibility
target_learners: final-year medical students
examples: The intervention group received an additional one-hour, lecture-only session introducing the systematic CXR interpretation checklist after the common two-hour base lecture

article_title: An E-Learning Program for Continuing Midwifery Education on Handling High-Risk Abuse Cases: A Pretest-Posttest Design.
citation: Baba Kaori, Kataoka Yaeko. (2023). An E-Learning Program for Continuing Midwifery Education on Handling High-Risk Abuse Cases: A Pretest–Posttest Design. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph20136317
title: Four-chapter e-learning program on handling high-risk child abuse cases for obstetric midwives and nurses
description: A self-paced e-learning program developed by the authors for midwifery continuing education, aligned with Japan's CLoCMiP clinical ladder. "The e-learning program comprised four chapters with several sections composed of short videos (5–10 min) and a quiz with multiple-choice questions with a single correct answer." Learners must answer correctly to proceed, and the program "took approximately 90 min to complete". Chapters cover abuse response and laws, prevention (risk factors, perinatal mental health, domestic violence), cooperation with related organizations, and roleplay.
requirements: Participants complete a pretest, the program, and a post-test online; an online support system was provided to help participants operate the program.
constraints: The article notes 20% of participants felt the program was too long, and about half of dropouts could not access the program after the pretest.
target_learners: obstetric midwives and nurses working in perinatal care in Japan
target_learning_goals: knowledge of abuse definitions, laws, and risk factors
responding to and supporting high-risk abuse cases
examples: Deployed with 71 obstetric midwives and nurses near Tokyo from December 2016 to July 2017 in a single-group pretest–posttest study; later used as CLoCMiP training during COVID-19 in 2020.

article_title: Developing a virtual reality (VR) application for practicing the ABCDE approach for systematic clinical observation.
citation: Berg H, Prasolova-Førland E, Steinsbekk A. (2023). Developing a virtual reality (VR) application for practicing the ABCDE approach for systematic clinical observation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04625-2
title: ABCDE VR application for self-instructed practice of systematic clinical observation
description: A fully immersive, interactive VR application built in Unity for commercially available goggles and hand controllers, letting inexperienced users practice the ABCDE approach alone or in multiplayer. Its solutions were categorised into "15 core features like onboarding, instructions, quiz, and feedback", including a virtual patient with haptic pulse feedback, a documentation tablet, and a three-star scoreboard. It was used in two RCTs with 578 first-year medical and nurse students.
requirements: Must be usable by players with no or little experience with head-mounted VR equipment and hand controllers
Requires commercially available VR goggles and hand controllers
constraints: Its use is limited to a basic introduction; other solutions are needed for practicing advanced ABCDE
Player movement is restricted by the physical area the player can move within, since teleportation was removed
target_learners: Medical and healthcare students at the beginning of their first semester
Health professionals inexperienced in the ABCDE approach and VR
target_learning_goals: Knowledge of which important clinical observations are included in the ABCDE approach
Carrying out ABCDE observations in the correct order and documenting them
examples: Players feel the heartbeat through the hand controller when placing their virtual hand on the patient's arm or chest

article_title: Adherence to the ABCDE approach in relation to the method of instruction: a randomized controlled simulation study.
citation: Linders M, Binkhorst M, Draaisma JMT, van Heijst AFJ, Hogeveen M. (2021). Adherence to the ABCDE approach in relation to the method of instruction: a randomized controlled simulation study. BMC Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12873-021-00509-0
title: Novel ABCDE adherence assessment tool with 24 APLS-derived items and trichotomous scoring
description: A purpose-built scoring instrument developed because no suitable tool existed: it incorporates "All 24 items of the ABCDE approach, as presented in the Dutch Advanced Pediatric Life Support (APLS) course manual", categorized under domains A–E. Items score 2, 1, or 0 points for adequate-and-timely, incomplete-or-out-of-sequence, and inadequate performance, with a maximum of 48 points, expressed as a percentage score. It demonstrated face and content validity and high intra-observer reliability.
requirements: Scoring requires trained video-based raters and detailed scoring instructions; items unperformable because help was rapidly summoned are classified as not assessable
constraints: Developed for the neonatal NALS simulation context; the authors state the instrument is also suitable for clinical patients
target_learners: neonatal healthcare providers undergoing NALS simulation training
target_learning_goals: measuring individual adherence to the ABCDE algorithm
examples: Used by one blinded researcher to score 65 percentage scores from videotaped simulation scenarios with three HD camera views combined into a 4-screen window

title: Validated ABC competency framework tables across three progression levels (student pre-internship, intern, nurse)
description: The artifact is a set of tables of competency frameworks for nursing care in airway, breathing/circulation and hemodynamic-state approaches in urgent situations, presented in figures for each ABC item. Each cell "reveals a competency framework to be demonstrated by the students within their level of progression", and frameworks are "present in greater number mainly at the initial levels of training", so "the level 3 (nurse) has consequently a higher level of empty cells". The progression levels were set by expert consensus based on the national curricular guidelines requiring a supervised internship in the last two semesters.
requirements: Requires the supervised curricular internship in the last two semesters of the undergraduate nursing course as the fundamental reference for students' progression levels.
target_learners: undergraduate nursing students
nurse trainees
target_learning_goals: systematic and rapid ABC assessment and immediate treatment in traumatic and non-traumatic emergencies
examples: Figures 1-3 present the frameworks prepared and validated for airway approach and hemodynamic state approach in situations of urgency.

citation: Dankbaar Mary E.W., Roozeboom Maartje Bakhuys, Oprins Esther A.P.B., Rutten Frans, van Merrienboer Jeroen J.G., van Saase Jan L.C.M., Schuit Stephanie C.E. (2017). Its design was based on a task analysis of the ABCDE approach, with cases validated by an expert panel and pilot tested with the target group. The game contained 6 regular adult patient cases, each solvable within 15 minutes and repeatable as often as desired, with a high-fidelity physiological model, direct feedback from patient monitor and virtual nurse, scores, and a high score list to stimulate competition.

article_title: Medical students' satisfaction with the Applied Basic Clinical Seminar with Scenarios for Students, a novel simulation-based learning method in Greece.
citation: Pantelidis P, Staikoglou N, Paparoidamis G, Drosos C, Karamaroudis S, Samara A, Keskinis C, Sideris M, Giannakoulas G, Tsoulfas G, Karagiannis A. (2016). description: The ABCS3 is a two-day simulation-based learning seminar for undergraduate medical students in Greece, built from "three core components: the case-based lectures, the ABCDE hands-on station, and the simulation-based clinical scenarios". Sixty full participants rotated through ten 30-minute scenarios in groups of six with two instructors, using mannequins, partial task simulators, and standardized patients, while 170 observers watched lectures and streamed scenarios. It was designed by the Scientific Society of Hellenic Medical Students with faculty revision.
requirements: Instructors in each scenario room to direct the process, enforce time limits, and structure team roles

constraints: Only 60 of 230 attendees could take part in the interactive hands-on scenarios; the remaining 170 observed via video live-streaming without interaction

title: Rotation-through-stations design: small groups cycle through all simulation scenarios in timed rounds
description: The seminar's core structural pattern is a timed rotation: the 60 full participants were "divided into 10 groups (I-X) of six people", each group starting at a different scenario, and "after 10 cycles of rotation (and 10 repeats of each scenario by different groups), all groups (I to X) had attended all the scenarios (Sc1 to Sc10)". Each 30-minute scenario room held six participants and two instructors, with an electronic alarm signalling rotation. This lets a large cohort experience every scenario with hands-on roles.
requirements: Enough parallel scenario rooms and instructor pairs to run all scenarios simultaneously
Strict 30-minute time limits enforced by instructors and an alarm signal
constraints: Requires a full-category cohort size that divides evenly into groups matching the number of scenarios; observers could not interact and only watched via live-stream
target_learners: undergraduate medical students working in small teams
target_learning_goals: team-based diagnostic and therapeutic decision-making under time pressure
examples: Groups I-X each completed all ten scenarios (trauma and suturing through orthopedic pelvic trauma) in one rotation cycle
